about: This synthetic 27-paragraph regional bus depot workshop review plants 9 domain_method defects, 1 denominator defect, 1 causal_claim defect and 1 overclaim defect (12 defective paragraphs in all), alongside 11 correct decoys and 4 plain correct paragraphs.

decoy_reasons.P04: Percentages are correct: 1,128 of 1,200 and 1,001 of 1,150 scheduled tasks, with the scheduled-task base stated.
decoy_reasons.P06: The rate is correct: 3 failures over 8,000 scheduled hours gives 0.375 per 1,000 unit-hours on the stated exposure.
decoy_reasons.P09: The causal word is supported: a randomly allocated 4 versus 4 lubrication trial is described, so the reduction claim is limited to the trial.
decoy_reasons.P11: The zero-failure statement is bounded to a stated six-month window with 4,000 scheduled hours, and makes no claim about the whole year.
decoy_reasons.P14: The per-lift rates are correct: 6 and 9 failures across the same 14 lifts give 0.43 and 0.64.
decoy_reasons.P16: The causal word is supported: a paired seal trial on 12 lifts is described, and the claim is limited to leak-related failures within it.
decoy_reasons.P19: Planned overhaul hours are correctly excluded from unplanned downtime, and the 22-hour mean is stated with its 5 events.
decoy_reasons.P21: The mean is over only 2 events, is explicitly stated as descriptive, and is not used to set an interval.
decoy_reasons.P23: The causal word is supported by a physical teardown of the failed part, which is direct evidence for the cause of the scoring.
decoy_reasons.P24: The percentage is correct on its stated base: 5 of 9 compressors had a failure, and the 5 failures fell on 5 different units.
decoy_reasons.P26: The limit statement is correct and bounded to the 12 sampled readings, none of which reached the 150 ppm limit.

why.P05: Two lathe failures in one year cannot establish a statistically significant improvement, so treating the drop from 3 to 2 as confirmation overstates what counts of this size allow.
why.P07: The 56% uses the 9 compressors as the base, whereas the share of all unplanned failures should use the 17 total failures, giving 29.4%.
why.P08: The detection score is entered on a scale where a higher score means easier detection, yet a higher detection score raises the risk priority number, so a well-detected failure mode is prioritised.
why.P10: A straight line fitted to three readings is projected six months beyond the last sample to predict the alert date, an extrapolation that the readings do not support.
why.P12: Inspection findings are counted as functional failures in the numerator, which inflates the brake tester failure rate from 0.375 to 1.25 per 1,000 unit-hours.
why.P15: Failure rates on different exposure bases (per 100 test cycles and per unit-year) are placed on one ranking, so the brake tester position is not comparable with the cranes.
why.P17: A fall in lift failures after a supplier change is presented as caused by the new grease, with no comparison group, which is a correlation presented as a cause.
why.P18: The preventive maintenance interval for a group of three lathes is set from one lathe's failure-free year, generalising a single unit's record to the group.
why.P20: The replacement decision rests on a simple payback from one year's repair cost, with no discounting or asset horizon, so it cannot support a capital approval.
why.P22: The 22-hour mean, pulled up by one 98-hour job, is used as the typical job length for crew planning, whereas the 3-hour median describes a typical job.
why.P25: The 30 planned re-certification hours are added to unplanned downtime, treating planned maintenance as failure time and raising the lift mean repair time from 16 to 21 hours.
why.P27: The 5 failures in 2025 and 4 in 2024 do not support the claim that the programme has removed failure risk or that monitoring can stop, so the statement overstates the evidence.
